newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland talks - what's on the table.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland talks - what's on the table.

text.p: Anglo-Irish negotiations on a political settlement for Northern Ireland are due to go ahead in September, based on a policy document worked out more than two years ago by the governments in London and Dublin.
They neither signal an end to British rule of the province, which the IRA and its Sinn Fein allies want, nor to prolong British rule indefinitely, as Protestant Unionists want.

Instead they propose that the two neighbouring states, with the two governments as guardians, work out a new set of relationships to blunt the edges of rival traditions and loyalites and to blur the border that separates them.
The proposals were contained in a "Framework Document" published by the British and Irish governments in February 1995 and distributed across the island of Ireland.

They are underpinned by the December 1993 Downing Street Declaration by the two governments which said Britain would not block the province joining the Irish republic if a majority wanted it. Protestants currently constitute a 60 per cent majority.
Ireland has promised a referendum on its constitutional claim to Northern Ireland as part of a balanced settlement to build trust and confidence.
Britain has said it could change is 1925 Government of Ireland act, under which Northern Ireland is part of Britain, in return.
Following are highlights of the framework document:
NORTH-SOUTH BODY

-- A North-South body will be set up comprising elected representatives from, and accountable to, a new Northern Ireland assembly and to the Irish Parliament. Its size and composition has not yet been determined.
-- The body will have executive, harmonising or consultative functions in matters that will be initially designated by the British and Irish parliaments.

Ministers say these might include tourism, roads and aspects of agriculture. While education as a whole would not be delegated to the North-South body, it could be given responsibility for harmonising teachers' qualifications.
-- Additional functions could later be designated, by agreement, by the Northern Ireland assembly and the Irish parliament.
-- All decisions of the body must be reached by consensus. Ministers said this requirement would be an important safeguard for both Irish nationalists and pro-British Protestants.
-- A parliamentary forum will be set up, comprising members of the Northern Ireland assembly and both houses of the Irish parliament, to consider matters of mutual interest.
CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGES

-- The Irish government will introduce and support proposals to change the country's constitution so that it no longer asserts a territorial claim to Northern Ireland contrary to the will of a majority of the province.
-- Ireland will recognise the legitimacy of whatever constitutional choice is freely exercised by a majority of the people of Northern Ireland.
-- The principle of consent in Northern Ireland will be enshrined for the first time in British legislation.
Britain will accept the will of the majority of the people to determine whether the province remains part of the United Kingdom or forms part of a united Ireland.
ANGLO-IRISH COOPERATION
-- Britain and Ireland will draw up a new, more broadly based agreement to develop and extend bilateral cooperation.
-- A standing inter-governmental conference will be created to consider matters of mutual interest, but not those transferred to the new political institutions.
-- Both governments will undertake to protect civil, political, social and cultural rights.
